title: 1 Kings 1:11–27
context: Nathan speaks to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon: Adonijah the son of Haggith reigns, and David does not know it. He asks her to receive his counsel, that she may save her own life and Solomon’s, and to go in and remind the king of his oath, “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.” Nathan will come in after her and confirm her words. Bathsheba enters the king’s room, where David is very old and Abishag the Shunammite is serving him. She bows, recites the oath, reports the feast and Solomon’s exclusion, and warns that when the king sleeps with his fathers she and Solomon will be considered criminals. While she is still talking, Nathan comes in, bows with his face to the ground, and asks whether David has said that Adonijah shall reign after him. He describes the sacrifice, the cry “Long live King Adonijah!”, and the fact that he, Zadok, Benaiah, and Solomon were not called, and he asks whether the king has shown his servants who should sit on the throne after him. The oath is first quoted here by Nathan and by Bathsheba; this book does not replay an earlier scene of the swearing. Abishag appears only as serving the king. Both traditions take David’s concern for the kingdom and the oath to Bathsheba as shared ground.

verses.text: Then Nathan spoke to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, saying, “Haven’t you heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith reigns, and David our lord doesn’t know it?
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan goes to Bathsheba with a question that is already news: “Haven’t you heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith reigns, and David our lord doesn’t know it?” The prophet names the bid as a present fact and the king’s ignorance as the danger.

Arminian readers hear counsel beginning in a real court crisis. Nathan does not wait for a vision in this verse; he speaks to the mother of Solomon about what Adonijah is already doing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise start from the report as a true state of affairs at court. Adonijah reigns in practice, and David does not know it.

Both traditions read Nathan’s approach as service to the king and to the oath that will now be recalled, not as a private plot against the throne.

verses.text: Now therefore come, please let me give you counsel, that you may save your own life and your son Solomon’s life.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan’s purpose is plain: “please let me give you counsel, that you may save your own life and your son Solomon’s life.” The risk is named as life itself, not merely a loss of influence.

Arminian readers take the warning as a genuine peril. If Adonijah’s bid stands, Bathsheba and Solomon may not survive, and Nathan asks her to act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same urgency. Counsel is given so that two lives may be saved, and the verse does not soften that stake.

Both traditions treat the danger as real. The next verses will show how the oath and the king’s word are brought to bear on it.

verses.text: Go in to King David, and tell him, ‘Didn’t you, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne”? Why then does Adonijah reign?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Bathsheba is to go in and ask, “Didn’t you, my lord the king, swear to your servant,” saying, “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne”? The oath is quoted in those words, and the question follows: why then does Adonijah reign?

Arminian readers take the remembered oath as a real obligation David freely swore. Nathan does not invent a new claim; he sends her to hold the king to words already spoken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also place the weight on the oath as spoken. “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne” is the word Bathsheba is to bring, and Adonijah’s present reign is set against it.

Both traditions treat that oath as shared ground for what follows. This book first quotes it here; it does not, in this chapter, show the earlier moment when it was sworn.

verses.text: Behold, while you are still talking there with the king, I will also come in after you and confirm your words.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan adds his own part: “Behold, while you are still talking there with the king, I will also come in after you and confirm your words.” The two testimonies are planned to stand together before David.

Arminian readers hear a wise and responsible confirmation, not a trick against the king. Nathan will say the same thing Bathsheba says, in David’s hearing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the second entrance as support for the oath, not as a rival counsel. The prophet will confirm her words while she is still speaking.

Both traditions read the plan as ordered testimony before the king.

verses.text: Bathsheba went in to the king in his room. The king was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bathsheba “went in to the king in his room.” David “was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.” Abishag is present as a servant in the room; the verse says nothing else about her.

Arminian readers keep that limit. The setting is the aged king’s room, and Abishag is serving, as chapter 1 has already described, without added intimacy or motive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the same restraint. The meeting takes place where the king is, and Abishag’s role here is service.

Both traditions describe the entrance as the narrator does. Bathsheba comes to speak; Abishag is mentioned only as serving the king.

verses.text: Bathsheba bowed and showed respect to the king. The king said, “What would you like?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Bathsheba “bowed and showed respect to the king.” He asks, “What would you like?” The queen mother approaches with honor, and David opens the hearing with a simple question.

Arminian readers hear a real audience, not a formality that changes nothing. She bows, and the king invites her to speak.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the respect and the question as the start of a genuine hearing. David is old, but he still receives her and asks what she wants.

Both traditions read the verse as court courtesy in a grave hour, shared ground before the oath is spoken again.

verses.text: She said to him, “My lord, you swore by the LORD your God to your servant, ‘Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.’
verses.arminianNotes:
She answers, “My lord, you swore by the LORD your God to your servant,” and she quotes the oath: “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.” The speech continues into the next verses.

Arminian readers hear her hold David to a vow made by the LORD his God. The oath is not flattery; it is a word she says he swore, and she places it first.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the appeal is to a sworn word, “by the LORD your God”, and to the same promise Nathan had given her to speak.

Both traditions take the oath itself as shared ground. Bathsheba’s first sentence is not a new political theory; it is the king’s own vow brought back to him.

verses.text: Now, behold, Adonijah reigns; and you, my lord the king, don’t know it.
verses.arminianNotes:
She continues, “Now, behold, Adonijah reigns; and you, my lord the king, don’t know it.” The contrast is sharp: a son already reigns, and the king has not been told.

Arminian readers hear a truthful report of David’s ignorance. The crisis has gone on without his knowledge, and she names that fact to his face.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to soften the line. Adonijah reigns, and David does not know it, just as Nathan had said to her.

Both traditions take the verse as the turning of the oath toward present danger. The king is being asked to see what has already begun.

verses.text: He has slain cattle and fatlings and sheep in abundance, and has called all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the captain of the army; but he hasn’t called Solomon your servant.
verses.arminianNotes:
She describes the feast: cattle, fatlings, and sheep in abundance, and a guest list of the king’s sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the captain of the army, “but he hasn’t called Solomon your servant.” The exclusion of Solomon is stated last and clearly.

Arminian readers hear a public claim already under way, and a deliberate leaving out of the son named in the oath.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same pattern already seen at En Rogel. Abiathar and Joab are with Adonijah; Solomon is not called.

Both traditions take the report as matching what the narrator has shown, brought now into David’s hearing.

verses.text: You, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, that you should tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
verses.arminianNotes:
She places the decision on David: “the eyes of all Israel are on you, that you should tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.” The people wait for the king’s word about the successor.

Arminian readers hear a real responsibility. David still has to speak, and Israel is looking to him to name who will sit after him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the throne as waiting on a public word from the king. The oath already exists, but the eyes of Israel are on David to declare it.

Both traditions treat this as shared concern for the kingdom: the successor must be told, not left to a feast at En Rogel.

verses.text: Otherwise it will happen, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be considered criminals.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The stakes are then named: “when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers,” she and Solomon “will be considered criminals.” The speech that began in verse 17 closes here.

Arminian readers take the warning as honest fear, not as exaggeration for effect. If David dies without a public word, mother and son may be treated as offenders.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same peril. The oath, if left unspoken before the people, will not protect them once the king sleeps with his fathers.

Both traditions keep the danger in view as she has stated it. The next movement is Nathan’s entrance, confirming her words.

verses.text: Behold, while she was still talking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, while she was still talking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.” The plan of verse 14 is carried out in the timing the prophet had named.

Arminian readers see a promised confirmation actually arriving. Nathan comes while she is still speaking, as he said he would.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the exactness of the entrance. The prophet comes in at the moment he had chosen, while the king is still hearing her.

Both traditions read the verse as the joining of the two witnesses, without turning the timing into a puzzle about providence versus counsel.

verses.text: They told the king, saying, “Behold, Nathan the prophet!” When he had come in before the king, he bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
The court announces, “Behold, Nathan the prophet!” He comes before the king and “bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground.” The prophet’s honor toward David is public and physical.

Arminian readers hear respect, not rivalry. Nathan bows to the king whose word he has come to seek.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the bow as the prophet’s place before the LORD’s anointed king. He does not enter as a master of the throne.

Both traditions describe the entrance as reverent. The hard questions will follow from a man already on his face before David.

verses.text: Nathan said, “My lord, King, have you said, ‘Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne’?
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan asks, “My lord, King, have you said, ‘Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne’?” He puts the rival claim in the form of a question about David’s own word.

Arminian readers hear a genuine inquiry. If David has said this, the court should know it; if he has not, the feast is running ahead of the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Nathan will not let a new successor be assumed in silence. The question is whether David has spoken this word, the same form of words used in the oath about Solomon.

Both traditions take the question as a test of the king’s will, not as Nathan crowning anyone himself.

verses.text: For he has gone down today, and has slain cattle, fatlings, and sheep in abundance, and has called all the king’s sons, the captains of the army, and Abiathar the priest. Behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’
verses.arminianNotes:
He reports the day’s events: Adonijah has gone down, slain cattle, fatlings, and sheep in abundance, and called the king’s sons, the captains of the army, and Abiathar. “Behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’”

Arminian readers hear a coronation cry already raised. The feast is not a private meal; the guests are saying, “Long live King Adonijah!”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the shout as a public claim. The captains and the priest are there, and the cry has the form used later for Solomon.

Both traditions let the report stand as confirmation of what Bathsheba has said, now in the prophet’s mouth.

verses.text: But he hasn’t called me, even me your servant, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
The excluded are named again: “he hasn’t called me, even me your servant, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon.” Nathan places himself, the other priest, the captain, and Solomon outside the feast.

Arminian readers hear the omission as evidence, not as wounded pride alone. The people David would be expected to consult have not been called.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same four names. The prophet, Zadok, Benaiah, and Solomon stand together in their absence from Adonijah’s table.

Both traditions read the verse as the other half of the guest list, preparing the question of verse 27.

verses.text: Was this thing done by my lord the king, and you haven’t shown to your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan closes, “Was this thing done by my lord the king, and you haven’t shown to your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?” The unit ends on that question, still waiting for David’s answer.

Arminian readers hear a real gap in the king’s communication. If the thing was done by David, his servants have not been shown the successor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the question open at the end of the passage. The throne after David has not yet been publicly assigned in the hearing of these servants.

Both traditions take David’s concern for the kingdom, and the oath already quoted, as the shared ground on which he must now speak.
